headline: IBM and Chicago ran a hard, encoded circuit, and certified how good the answer was
dek: A 64-qubit circuit with 314 T gates, encoded in 76 physical qubits, with gate errors about ten times lower once runs that flagged an error were thrown out. The new part is not the size. It is the certificate.

source.name: arXiv
source.title: Sampling hard circuits with verifiably high fidelity (arXiv:2607.25941, v3, 2 September 2026)

body_html:
A team from IBM and the University of Chicago ran a 64-qubit circuit containing 314 T gates, encoded across 76 physical qubits in a code that detects errors. Runs in which the code flagged an error were discarded, and on the runs that remained the effective gate error rate came out about ten times lower than the hardware's own. The paper certifies a lower bound on the fidelity of the final state: 0.349, with 95% confidence.

The first version of the paper, posted on 28 July, described a 70-qubit circuit with 468 T gates on 97 physical qubits. The authors revised it in September. This story first ran with the July figures, and called the circuit error-corrected, which it was not in either version (see below).

The number worth holding is the word verifiably in the paper's title. Sampling experiments have always had the same weakness: the output is hard to produce and equally hard to check, so "we did something a classical computer cannot" has historically rested on an argument rather than a receipt. This work comes with a certificate for its fidelity. The certificate depends on assumptions about the device, though the paper argues they are much weaker than the ones the usual benchmarks need.

The T-gate count is the second thing to notice. T gates are the expensive ones: Clifford operations alone are classically simulable, so a circuit's difficulty lives in its non-Clifford content, and on a fault-tolerant machine those gates are paid for by magic-state distillation. 314 of them is a real workload, not a demonstration of two.

What this does NOT mean

  • It is not a useful application. The circuit was chosen because it is hard to simulate, not because anyone wants its output. Nothing here schedules a delivery fleet, designs a molecule, or breaks a key.
  • It is error detection, not error correction. The code notices errors and those runs are thrown away; it does not repair them. That works while enough runs survive, and it gets more expensive as circuits grow, which is why correction, not detection, is the long-term goal.
  • "Beyond classical simulation" is a moving line, not a wall. That boundary is defined by the best classical method anyone has published, and it has moved in both directions before — Google's 2019 Sycamore claim has been matched, beaten, and re‑matched by classical simulation in the years since. A result past today's line can be behind tomorrow's without anybody having done anything wrong.
  • The qubit counts here are not logical-qubit counts. The 64 qubits are encoded for error detection, not error-corrected logical qubits, and counts like these are specific to one code and one circuit. They do not port.
concept_card_html:
Concepts in this story

Each of these is already explained on SymbiQ. Depth chips say how deep the explanation goes.

  • logical qubitplainOne reliable qubit built out of many unreliable ones. The only qubit count that means anything.
  • quantum error correctionplainSpreading one fragile qubit across many so the machine can find mistakes without ever looking at the answer.
  • magic-state factoriesformalClifford gates alone are classically simulable, so universality is smuggled in via a purified magic state -- consume several noisy copies, distill out fewer higher-fidelity ones.
  • NISQ & quantum advantage experimentsplainNoisy Intermediate-Scale Quantum, the era the field is actually in -- and the still-unsettled tug-of-war between Google's 2019 Sycamore claim and classical simulations that have matched, lost to, and matched it again since.
